newsitem.title: USA: U.S. congressman to hold hearings on Swiss banks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. congressman to hold hearings on Swiss banks.

text.p: A U.S. congressman said on Friday he will hold a hearing next month on assets deposited in Swiss banks by victims of the Nazi Holocaust.

The Dec. 11 hearing will also explore the role of Swiss banks, including the central bank, in the buying and selling of Nazi gold during the Second World War, House Banking Committee Chairman James Leach said.
"The issue of finding and returning to the Holocaust victims and their surviving relatives what is rightfully theirs is not a narrow concern," Leach, a Republican from Iowa, said in a statement.

Witnesses will include Paul Volcker, former chairman of the Federal Reserve, who heads a commission to investigate the amount of assets of Holocaust victims in Swiss banks. The Volcker panel was set up by Swiss banks and Jewish groups.
Also scheduled to testify is Thomas Borer, deputy secretary general of the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, who is coordinating the government's task force on the assets of Nazi victims.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, a Republican from New York, held a hearing last month at which he said the Swiss government used Jewish assets to compensate its own citizens for properties taken from them. Switzerland has denied D'Amato's assertion.

Leach said the "profoundness" of the issue, the relationship of the United States with Europe and the intertwined nature of international banking meant "Congress has no decent option except to review the lessons which emerge when light is shined in history's dark corners."
On Tuesday, the Swiss government denied reports it ordered financial institutions to waive secrecy laws and cooperate in a probe of how the Nazis used Swiss banks during the war.

The World Jewish Congress said earlier it was told by the Swiss Federal Council, the country's collective presidency, that all financial institutions had been ordered to make their records from 1933 to 1945 available to state investigators.

But the Swiss Foreign Ministry told Reuters no such decision was made by the government, which under current law is not able to order banks and other financial groups, such as life insurers or asset managers, to throw open their books.
Instead, a ministry spokesman said parliament was in the early stages of considering a proposal that would allow a government probe with powers to demand financial records.

Legislators expect to debate the bill next year. If approved by both chambers, it could be passed by the Federal Council by year's end and a national referendum vote could then be necessary before the law could take effect.
